claim: LLM-as-a-judge evaluates AI outputs by having a judge model score a candidate response against a predefined rubric and return a structured verdict, rather than comparing text overlap.
stance_target: feasibility of automated adversarial/quality review pipelines in an AI software factory
quoted_support: LLM-as-a-judge is an LLM evaluation method where a large language model reads a prompt, and the AI-generated response is evaluated. The judge model compares the response against a predefined rubric and returns a structured assessment.

claim: Agent-as-a-judge extends single-pass LLM-as-a-judge by orchestrating multi-step evaluation: retrieving evidence, executing tools, consulting multiple models before producing a verdict.
stance_target: adversarial model review pillar requiring multi-step verification beyond single-pass scoring
quoted_support: Agent-as-a-judge goes a step further by orchestrating multiple evaluation steps: retrieving evidence, executing tools, or consulting multiple models, before reaching a verdict.

claim: LLM judges exhibit self-preference bias, scoring their own generations higher than human reviewers do.
stance_target: zero-hallucination/quality-control reliability of using a single model as both generator and judge
scope_conditions: 2024 study of GPT-4 and similar evaluator models
quoted_support: A self-preference bias is documented in a 2024 study, LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations, which explains that GPT-4 (and similar LLM evaluator models) score their own outputs higher than human reviewers do.
entities: LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations

claim: LLM judges systematically over-weight response length, rewarding longer answers even when length is unrelated to quality, per the Length-Controlled AlpacaEval paper (2024).
stance_target: reliability of naive LLM-as-a-judge scoring for code/content quality gates
quoted_support: The 2024 Length-Controlled AlpacaEval paper found that many LLM judges over-weight response length, rewarding longer answers even when length has nothing to do with quality.

claim: LLM judge scores drift after judge model version upgrades even when prompt and rubric are unchanged, making cross-release comparisons unreliable unless the judge is frozen for the evaluation cycle.
stance_target: need for rigid, version-pinned evals in a continuously operating agent factory
quoted_support: Keep the judge model and prompt fixed for the length of an evaluation run. Even small prompt revisions or model upgrades can change scoring behavior.

claim: CodeJudgeBench benchmarked 26 LLM judges across code generation, code repair, and unit test generation tasks, finding pairwise comparison improves judge accuracy for selecting the better of two code responses.
stance_target: feasibility of LLM-judge-based code quality gating in a software factory pipeline
quoted_support: In CodeJudgeBench, Hongchao Jiang and colleagues benchmarked 26 LLM judges across code generation, code repair, and unit test generation.

claim: LLM judges cannot reliably detect hallucinations absent access to trusted reference material or retrieval, treating plausible fabricated claims as factual.
stance_target: zero-hallucination quality control relying solely on unsupported LLM-as-judge scoring
quoted_support: An LLM judge cannot reliably detect hallucinations unless it has access to trusted reference material or a retrieval system to check. Without supporting evidence, it may treat plausible statements as factual.
